subject: Cognitive Science
title: Loss Aversion
description: A quick win: understand Loss Aversion.

hook.text: Losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good. Same amount, different emotional weight.

buildup.text: Loss aversion: losses loom larger than gains. This asymmetry drives much of human decision-making.

discovery.text: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory replaced expected utility: people weigh losses roughly 2x more than gains.

twist.text: This makes people reject fair bets. A 50/50 chance to win $120 or lose $100? Most say no.

climax.text: Insurance, warranties, and money-back guarantees all profit from loss aversion—pay to avoid losing.

punchline.text: Fear of loss outweighs hope for gain.

quiz.question: What does loss aversion predict?
options: Losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel good

details.summary: Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains feel good. This asymmetry, called loss aversion, powerfully shapes decisions: people will take irrational risks to avoid losses and reject favorable bets that involve any chance of losing.
details.whyItMatters: Loss aversion drives everything from investment mistakes to policy resistance. Understanding it explains why people cling to the status quo and fear change disproportionately.
takeaways: Losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel good
Loss aversion leads to irrational risk-taking to avoid losses
Kahneman and Tversky identified it as core to prospect theory

faq.question: How does loss aversion affect investment decisions?
faq.answer: Investors hold losing stocks too long hoping to break even and sell winning stocks too early to lock in gains. This disposition effect directly results from loss aversion. It consistently reduces portfolio returns compared to rational selling strategies.

faq.question: Is loss aversion culturally universal?
faq.answer: Loss aversion appears across cultures but its magnitude varies. Some hunter-gatherer societies show weaker loss aversion, suggesting both biological and cultural influences. The core asymmetry between losses and gains seems universal, but context and framing modulate its strength.
